title: Form and sound (section 26)
hook: those who see me by form or seek me by sound walk the wrong road (as Müller renders the verse)

segments.voice: Yesterday, no beings freed: the Tathagata helps without the thought, I set them free. Your line: no one to free. Did you manage one kind thing you didn't mention? Day one thousand one hundred forty-three.

Outside a bookstore, a line wraps around the block. A famous writer is signing tonight. A young man near the front has waited three hours. He gets his photo, a handshake, the sound of the writer saying his name. He walks away glowing. Then a friend asks him what the books are about, and he laughs. He hasn't read them. He has seen the writer's face and heard the writer's voice, and he has missed the writer completely. Section twenty-six of the Diamond Sutra puts this same mistake in a short verse, and it aims the verse at the Buddha himself. Today: form and sound.
screen: `A LINE AROUND THE BLOCK.` → `A FACE, A VOICE, A PHOTO.` → `HE NEVER READ THE BOOKS.`

segments.voice: First, the question, one more time. The Buddha asks Subhuti whether the Tathagata can be recognized by his bodily marks, the signs tradition says a great being bears. The sutra has asked this before, and here it adds a sharp reason for the answer no. If the marks were enough, the Buddha says, then a wheel-turning king, a world ruler who bears the same marks, would be a Tathagata too. A body can look the part and not be the thing. Second, the verse. The Buddha speaks it in a few lines. In paraphrase: those who see me by my form, and those who follow me by my voice, have set out on a wrong road. They will not see me. Form is what the eye catches. Sound is what the ear catches. Both are real, and both are the outside. Third, the second half of the verse, which is easy to skip. The Buddhas are to be seen from the Dharma, it says; their body is the Dharma. And the nature of the Dharma isn't something the mind can grab as an object. So the verse closes one road and points down another: you meet the Tathagata where the teaching is lived, not where the outline of a body stands. Fourth, what the verse doesn't say. A Buddhist temple may hold images and chanting. Read in a room like that, the verse doesn't ask anyone to tear the images down or fall silent. It asks where the looking stops. A statue can be a doorway. The mistake is to stand in the doorway admiring the frame.
screen: `ARE THE MARKS ENOUGH?` · `NOT BY FORM, NOT BY VOICE.` · `SEEN FROM THE DHARMA.` · `A DOORWAY, NOT THE ROOM.` · then, large: `NOT BY FORM OR SOUND.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: look past form once. Settle, and breathe. If there's a photo near you of someone you care about, or an image of the Buddha, or just a cup, let your eyes rest on it. First, take in the form: the shape, the colors, the edges. Let that be complete. Then, without looking away, ask quietly: what is this beyond its shape? For a person, maybe the way they laugh, or something they taught you. For a cup, the hands that made it, the tea it held. Let the form soften while the looking goes on. The bell holds the time.
Form and sound. The eye's catch and the ear's catch: the verse in section twenty-six says the Tathagata isn't found there, but seen from the Dharma. Today's word.
Your line: not by form or sound. Today, when a familiar voice reaches you, listen once past its sound to what the person is actually asking for. Day one thousand one hundred forty-three.

howItsDone: Mahayana Buddhists chant and study the Diamond Sutra, and some communities recite its verse on form and sound by heart; it's read alongside the images and chanting of temple life, as a reminder of what they point to.

fork.setup: you're Subhuti. the Buddha asks: can the Tathagata be recognized by his bodily marks? what does the sutra answer?
options: no: a wheel-turning king has the marks too
only by the marks and the voice together
fork.reveal: the marks aren't enough; then comes the verse: whoever sees him by form or follows him by voice is on a wrong road.

original.note: Sanskrit and Pali: form, shape, what the eye sees; the 'form' of the verse in section 26.

trapdoor: what you thought: Buddhists aren't supposed to look at images of the Buddha.
what it means: form and voice are the outside; the verse says the Tathagata is seen from the Dharma.
what a scholar hears: the verse sets seeing by form against seeing from the Dharma, and calls the Buddhas' body the Dharma-body.

notes: The section 26 verse is paraphrased, not quoted: the outline cites Max Müller's rendering, but his exact wording was not verified. A Keeper may wish to supply Müller's text verbatim.

Versions differ on whether Subhuti first answers yes and is corrected (Kumarajiva's Chinese) or answers no at once (the Sanskrit Müller used); the script avoids saying which. Check the wheel-turning king (cakravartin) detail.

The second half of the verse (the Buddhas seen from the Dharma; the Dharma-body; the Dharma's nature not graspable) is absent from some Chinese versions; the script says only that the verse has it. Confirm.
Practice suggests an image of the Buddha as one option; confirm this is respectful.
